payload.text: A pinhole camera uses a small hole and a projection surface to create an image by allowing light from only one direction to reach each point on the surface.
The pinhole camera model explains how a simple aperture projects a scene onto a surface, foundational for understanding image formation in cameras.

Perhaps the simplest camera is a pinhole camera. A pinhole camera requires a light-tight enclosure, a small hole that lets light pass, and a projection surface where one senses or views the illumination intensity as a function of position. @fig-wallpicture (b) shows the geometry of a scene, the pinhole, and a projection surface (wall). For any given point on the projection surface, the light that falls there comes from only from one direction, along the straight line joining the surface position and the pinhole. This creates an image of what's in the world on the projection plane.

payload.prompt: In a pinhole camera, for a given point on the projection surface, the light arriving there comes from…

payload.explanation_correct: Right — a pinhole admits only one ray per surface point, which is exactly what creates a sharp image.
payload.explanation_wrong: Look again at the geometry: each surface point sees light only along the line that passes through the (infinitely small) pinhole.

payload.text: Think about what the pinhole physically restricts. How many rays from the scene can land on any single point of the projection surface, if the hole is one point in space?
